What Meta’s Georgia Data Center Teaches Us About Ethical AI

Artificial intelligence may seem virtual, but every AI model depends on physical infrastructure, real resources, and real communities.

Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) is frequently associated with ethical concerns such as algorithmic bias, privacy violations, surveillance, and misinformation. While these issues dominate public discussions, they often overlook a less visible but equally important component of AI: the physical infrastructure that makes AI possible.

Large language models, chatbots, recommendation system, and generative AI applications depend on massive data centers. These facilities require substantial amounts of electricity, water, cooling systems, land, and computing resources to operate. As technology companies invest billions of dollars into AI development, the environmental and social consequences of these facilities are becoming increasingly significant. This shift raises an important question:

Should AI ethics focus only on the behavior of algorithms, or should it also consider the infrastructure that supports them?

Can AI truly be considered ethical if the infrastructure supporting it harms local communities?

This question sits at the heart of the controversy surrounding the Meta data center project in Georgia, a case that reveals why AI ethics must extend beyond algorithms and into the physical world.

The Families Behind the Headlines

For many people, AI is associated with innovation and technological progress.

For several families living near the Meta Stanton Springs Data Center, however, the conversation became much more personal. According to legal filings, four Georgia families alleged that construction activities associated with the project negatively affected their well water and quality of life.

Residents reported discolored water, sediment contamination, reduced water pressure, dust pollution, construction noise, and declining property values. These concerns were later included in legal actions against the project. [USA Today] The homeowners claimed they felt trapped because their properties relied on private wells and could not easily be abandoned. [usatoday.com], [greyjournal.net]

Meta has denied responsibility and cited studies suggesting its activities were unlikely to have caused the reported problems. The legal case remains disputed. [usatoday.com]

However, regardless of how the lawsuit is resolved, the controversy highlights an important ethical issue:

Who bears the costs of AI innovation?

Millions of people benefit from AI-powered services, yet the environmental and community impacts of the infrastructure supporting those systems are often concentrated in a few local communities.

Looking Beyond the Algorithm

A major theme in Luciano Floridi’s work is that technology should be evaluated based on its effects on society, not simply whether it works efficiently.

Too often, organizations focus on whether an AI system performs well technically while overlooking broader consequences for stakeholders.

In this case, the ethical challenge is not an algorithm making a biased decision. The ethical challenge is the impact of AI infrastructure itself.

The controversy reminds us that ethical AI is not only about what algorithms do. It is also about what must be built so those algorithms can exist.

Beneficence: Does AI Create More Good Than Harm?

One of Luciano Floridi’s central ethical principles is Beneficence, which asks whether technology promotes human well-being.

Looking at the Meta project, there are undeniable benefits:

  •	New technology investment
  •	Economic development
  •	Job creation
  •	Expanded digital infrastructure
  •	Increased AI capability

The facility supports systems that may improve productivity, communication, and access to digital services for millions of people.From this perspective, the project contributes positively to society.

However, beneficence alone is not enough. An ethical evaluation must also ask whether those benefits come at an unacceptable cost.

Technology can generate significant value while still creating ethical concerns for specific communities.

Non-Maleficence: The Duty to Avoid Harm

The second principle, non-maleficence, is often summarized as “do no harm.” This principle becomes particularly important when examining the concerns raised by Georgia residents.

Whether or not investigations ultimately establish direct responsibility, the complaints themselves reveal why organizations should carefully assess environmental risks before construction begins. [usatoday.com], [greyjournal.net]

Ethically responsible organizations should not simply wait until a problem occurs. Instead, they should ask:

•	What could go wrong? 
•	Who could be affected? 
•	How can potential harm be minimized?

This is especially important for Artificial Intelligence because many discussions focus exclusively on digital harm while ignoring physical harm to communities.

Responsible AI begins long before an algorithm is trained. It starts when organizations decide how and where to build the infrastructure that powers AI.

Justice: The Most Important Question

Among all ethical concepts, Justice may be the most significant for understanding this controversy. Justice concerns fairness.

In the Meta case, there is an apparent imbalance:

Benefits
•	Global users gain access to AI technologies.
•	Businesses gain productivity advantages.
•	Companies gain revenue and competitive advantages.

Risks
•	Local communities experience the environmental impacts.
•	Residents face uncertainty about water resources.
•	Property owners absorb potential quality-of-life disruptions.

This creates a classic ethical dilemma.

Is it fair for a small number of residents to absorb environmental risks so that society as a whole can enjoy the benefits of AI ?

Even when a project complies with regulations, questions of justice may remain unresolved.

Why Transparency and Accountability Matter

Another important principle is Explicability, which includes both Transparency and Accountability.

When concerns emerged about the Georgia facility, residents wanted answers:

•	How much water would the facility require ?
•	What environmental studies have been conducted ?
•	How would impacts be monitored ?
•	Who would be responsible if harm occurred ?

These are fundamental questions about transparency and accountability.

Without access to information, communities cannot meaningfully participate in decisions that affect them. Without accountability, public trust becomes difficult to maintain.

Transparency is not merely a communication strategy. It is an ethical obligation.

Soft Ethics vs. Legal Compliance

One of Floridi’s most influential ideas is the distinction between regulation and ethics.

A company may comply with every applicable law and still face legitimate ethical criticism.

This is where Soft Ethics becomes important. Soft ethics asks organizations to go beyond minimum legal requirements and consider broader societal responsibilities.

For example, even if regulations were technically satisfied, organizations could still choose to:

•	Conduct independent environmental monitoring.
•	Share sustainability reports publicly.
•	Consult communities before expansion.
•	Establish long-term accountability programs.

The key question becomes:

What should we do? " rather than " What should organizations do? What are organizations legally allowed to do?

This mindset represents the foundation of responsible innovation.

AI Governance and Ethical Impact Assessments

The controversy also illustrates the importance of AI Governance and Ethical Impact Assessments (EIAs).

AI governance involves policies, oversight mechanisms, and accountability structures used to guide the development and deployment of AI systems.

An Ethical Impact Assessment provides a proactive way to evaluate risks before projects are approved.

Had such an assessment been more visible, it might have examined:

•	Groundwater impacts
•	Community concerns
•	Sustainability challenges
•	Long-term monitoring requirements
•	Stakeholder participation mechanisms
The goal of an Ethical Impact Assessment is not to stop innovation. It is to ensure innovation occurs responsibly.

Sustainability: The Missing AI Ethics Conversation

The most important lesson from this case is the growing importance of Sustainability.

For years, AI ethics focused primarily on fairness, privacy, and bias. Those topics remain important.

However, AI systems now require unprecedented computing power, which means unprecedented demands for energy, water, and infrastructure.

As AI capabilities grow, sustainability can no longer be treated as a separate environmental discussion.

It is an AI ethics discussion.

An AI system cannot be considered fully ethical if the infrastructure supporting it creates unsustainable environmental pressures.

The Meta controversy reminds us that the future of AI depends not only on better algorithms, but also on responsible resource management.

Final Thoughts

The controversy surrounding the Meta Stanton Springs Data Center challenges us to rethink what ethical AI really means.

Using the concepts of Beneficence, Non-maleficence, Justice, Explicability, Soft Ethics, AI Governance, Ethical Impact Assessment, and Sustainability, this case demonstrates that ethical concerns can emerge long before an AI system interacts with a user.

The families who filed complaints were not questioning the accuracy of an algorithm. They were questioning whether technological progress was occurring in a way that respected their community, environment, and quality of life. [usatoday.com], [greyjournal.net]

Ultimately, the lesson is simple:

The future of ethical AI depends not only on building smarter systems, but also on building them responsibly.

References

• Luciano Floridi, (2023). The Ethics of Artificial Intelligence: Principles, Challenges, and Opportunities. Oxford University Press.

• Reports regarding allegations by residents near Meta Stanton Springs Data Center, concerning groundwater disruption, well-water contamination, property impacts, and community concerns related to the Meta Stanton Springs Data Center. [usatoday.com], [greyjournal.net]

• Four Georgia families have filed a 180-page lawsuit against Meta and local development officials, alleging that the construction of the Meta Stanton Springs Data Center has contaminated their private well water and ruined their quality of life.

Media reference links are listed below:

• https://greyjournal.net/hustle/work-tech/meta-data-center-georgia-water-crisis/

• https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/state/georgia/2026/09/02/meta-sued-by-georgia-families-following-construction-of-data-center/91578594007/

• https://www.reddit.com/r/Georgia/comments/1xcszs4/4_georgia_families_sue_meta_claim_data_center/

• https://www.facebook.com/100083241103501/videos/metas-massive-data-center-in-georgia-has-raised-serious-concerns-among-nearby-re/2424575424617973/

• https://www.ajc.com/news/2026/09/georgia-families-sue-meta-accuse-its-data-center-of-tainting-their-water/

• https://www.youtube.com/shorts/0mxeI1hhn-0

• https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CQcLJNwN1j0

• https://www.usatoday.com/videos/news/politics/2026/05/22/aoc-presses-epa-data-center-water-contamination/90217057007/

Skills Demonstrated:

AI Ethics Analysis, AI Governance, Sustainability Assessment, Ethical Impact Assessment (EIA), Stakeholder Analysis, Risk Assessment, and Evidence-Based Research.

Key Strengths:

Critical Thinking, Strategic Decision-Making, Technical Communication, and the ability to evaluate AI systems through environmental, social, business, and governance perspectives.
title: The Hidden Cost of AI

Data Analytics Beyond the Dashboard

Introduction

Many people associate data analytics with dashboards, reports, and charts. Yet the dashboard is often the smallest part of the analyst’s work.

Behind every metrics, trend line, and KPI (Key Performance Indicator) lies a series of questions, investigations, validations, and business decisions. Before a chart reaches an executive meeting, an analyst has already spent hours in understanding the problem, examining the data, and determining whether the results can be trusted.

A dashboard is the final output. Analysis is everything that happens before it.

The Dashboard Is the Destination, Not the Journey

Most stakeholders see:

Dashboard
    ↓
Insight
    ↓
Decision

A data analyst sees:

Business Question
        ↓
Requirements
        ↓
Data Collection
        ↓
Data Quality Checks
        ↓
Analysis
        ↓
Validation
        ↓
Visualization
        ↓
Insights
        ↓
Decision

The dashboard rarely creates the insight. The investigation behind it does.

Every Number Starts With a Question

Lets assume a business scenario.

A dashboard shows: Revenue is down by 12%. Most people stop there.

Here is what a Data Analyst comes, and starts asking: WHY ?

Then the investigation expands:

Revenue ↓
   ├── Product Mix?
   ├── Customer Retention?
   ├── Market Conditions?
   ├── Pricing Changes?
   ├── Seasonal Effects?
   └── Data Quality Issues?

The Invisible Work Nobody Talks About

Before Building Any Dashboard, the data analyst performs below tasks:

✓ Understanding requirements
✓ Clarifying business definitions
✓ Identifying data sources
✓ Checking missing values
✓ Resolving inconsistencies
✓ Validating calculations
✓ Reviewing assumptions
✓ Testing results

An inaccurate dashboard created quickly is far less valuable than a reliable dashboard created thoughtfully.

The Tools Behind the Decisions

1. SQL

Used when analysts need answers from large datasets.

SELECT Region,
       SUM(Sales)
FROM Orders
GROUP BY Region;

Purpose:

  1. Find data
  2. Filter information
  3. Investigate patterns
  4. Answer business questions
2. Excel

Excel is often underestimated. However, its a good tool used for:

  1. Validation
  2. Quick analysis
  3. Comparisons
  4. Ad-hoc requests

Many investigations begin analysing data through Excel long before formal reporting starts.

3. Power BI

Used for communication.

Raw Data → Information → Understanding

Power BI does not create business value because it makes charts. It creates value because it helps people understand what the data is telling them.

A chart alone is not the goal. The goal is helping stakeholders move from data to understanding and from understanding to action.

Charts display data. Understanding creates value. Power BI helps bridge that gap by turning complex information into insights that people can act upon.

4. Python

Used when analysis becomes repetitive or complex.

import pandas as pd

This tool is helpful for :

  1. Automation
  2. Forecasting
  3. Large datasets
  4. Advanced analysis
5. Where AI Fits Into the Process

This should feel balanced, not overly promotional.

Traditional Workflow

Question
   ↓
Gather Data
   ↓
Analyze
   ↓
Build Visuals

Modern Workflow

Question
   ↓
AI Assists
   ↓
Analysis
   ↓
Human Validation
   ↓
Decision
6. AI can speed up analytical work, but responsibility for interpretation remains with the analyst.

AI provides assistance and provides judgment in below tasks:

  • SQL generation
  • Formula suggestions
  • Documentation support
  • Visualization recommendations
  • Data summarization
7. The Decision Layer

A Dashboard anaswers:

What happened?

A strong analyst helps to answer:

Why did it happen?
What should we do next?
What risks should we consider?

For example, if Sales ↑ 18% , good reporting would be Sales have increased.

A good Analyst would advise:

  1. Sales increased because
  2. A new customer segment responded positively
  3. A promotional campaign
8. The Most Valuable Skill Is Not Coding

Technical skills matter:

SQL , Power BI , Python, Excel, AI Tools

The strongest skills the analysts consistently demonstrate are:

  1. Curiosity
  2. Critical Thinking
  3. Business Understanding
  4. Communication
  5. Problem Solving
Tools help analysts access data. Questions help analysts create value.

Conclusion

The dashboard is often the part everyone remembers, but it represents only the final stage of a much larger process. Behind every metric lies a series of questions, validations, investigations, and decisions that transform raw information into meaningful action.

A dashboard can tell you what happened. An analyst helps explain why it happened and what should happen next.

Skills Strengthened:

  • Data Investigation and Analytical Thinking
  • Business Communication and Decision Support
description: The Decisions Behind Every Data Point
title: Behind Dashboards

content:
Building Trust Through Data

Introduction

When I first began my data analytics journey, I believed trust came from accurate calculations, dashboards, and technical skills. Over time, I realized that trust is not created by data alone. It is built when people understand the information, believe the evidence, and feel confident using trust to make decisions.

Trust is the bridge between data and action.

An analyst may create an excellent report, but if stakeholders do not trust the findings, the analysis has little impact.

Analytics become valuable when it helps people move from opinions to evidence-based decisions.

Opinion → Evidence → Understanding → Decision

What does that mean?

• Opinion : What people think or assume

• Evidence : Data, facts, and analysis

• Understanding: Interpreting what the evidence means

• Decision: Action based on that understanding

Everyone Wants an Answer

Organizations rely on analytics because they need answers.

• Why are customers leaving?

• Why are sales declining?

• Why are costs increasing?

• Why is a project underperforming?

• What should we do next?

When these questions arise, there is often a pressure to find answers quickly. Stakeholders want direction, managers want clarity, and decisionmakers want confidence. However, analytics is not about finding the fastest answer. It is about finding the most reliable answer.

A good analyst focuses on evidence rather than assumptions.

The pressure to provide answers quickly should never outweigh the responsibility to provide answers accurately.

For example, a 10% drop in sales does not automatically mean there is a product problem. It could be caused by competition, seasonality, market conditions, or changing customer preferences.

Sales ↓
   ↓
Product?
Competition?
Market Conditions?
Seasonality?

When sales decrease, a good analyst doesn’t immediately assume they know the reason. Instead, they investigate multiple possible causes.

Different People See Data Differently

The same data can mean different things to different people. For instance, consider a customer satisfaction score that falls from 88% to 83%.

Manager's Perspective
  ↓
Same Data
  ↓
Team's Perspective
  ↓
Executive Perspective

Imagine customer satisfaction decreases by 5%. A manager may focus on the decline. A project team may highlight recent improvements. An executive may compare results to industry benchmarks.

The analyst’s role is not to choose sides. The analyst’s role is to present evidence clearly, explain context, and help stakeholders understand what the data suggests.

Data does not change depending on who views it, but its interpretation does.

This is why context matters.

Data + Context = Meaning

Without context, numbers can be misunderstood. With context, they become insights.

Numbers rarely tell the whole story by themselves. Context is what transforms information into understanding.

Information vs. Reassurance

A challenge that analysts often face is that people do not always seek information. Sometimes they seek reassurance.

What People Want → Validation
What Analysts Provide → Evidence

A stakeholder may hope the results support a recent decision. A team may hope a project is performing well. A manager may expect data to validate an existing assumption.In these situations, analysts must remain objective.

The purpose of analytics is not to tell people what they want to hear. The purpose of analytics is to help people understand what the evidence indicates.

The role of an analyst is not to confirm assumptions. It is to evaluate them.

Strong analysts challenge ideas when necessary and support them when justified.

For Example:

Expected Result: Profit Increase ↑

Actual result: Revenue ↑ Costs ↑↑ Profit ↓

The data may tell a very different story than expected.

This responsibility becomes especially important when results differ from expectations. Trust is strengthened when stakeholders know the conclusions are based on evidence rather than preference.

Data Surprises Us

If data simply confirms what everyone already believes, little learning occurs. Growth often begins when evidence challenges assumptions.

For example: Imagine a company believes customers aged 18-25 are its primary audience. After analysis, it discovers the largest customer segment is between ages 41-55.

This insight may completely change future marketing strategies. As analysts we should view unexpected results as opportunities rather than problems.

An unexpected finding may reveal:
• Missing information
• New trends
• Hidden risks
• Emerging opportunities
• Incorrect assumptions

The most valuable insights often arise when the data tells a different story than the one we expected to hear.

Trust grows when analysts follow evidence wherever it leads, even when the destination is surprising.

Building Credibility Through Consistency

Trust is not built through a single dashboard or report. It develops through consistency. Stakeholders build confidence in analysts who repeatedly demonstrate professionalism, objectivity, and reliability.

Consistency
  ↓
Credibility
  ↓
Confidence
  ↓
Trust

Consistency means:

• Using reliable methods

• Applying the same standards

• Explaining conclusions clearly

• Supporting findings with evidence

• Acknowledging uncertainty

Even when stakeholders disagree with the outcome, they are more likely to trust a process that is transparent and repeatable.

Trust is rarely earned through one impressive report. It is earned through repeated reliability.

Reliable Process + Clear Communication + Objective Analysis = Credibility

Over time, credibility becomes one of an analyst’s most valuable assets.

Accepting That Not Every Answer Is Perfect

One of the biggest surprises for me was learning that analytics is often about reducing uncertainty rather than eliminating it.

One of the biggest surprises for me was learning that analytics is often about reducing uncertainty rather than eliminating it.

Perfect Information ✗

Better Information ✓

Many decisions must be made even when information is incomplete. Example A retail company wants to forecast holiday sales.

Unknowns include: • Customer Demand • Weather • Competition • Economic Conditions

No analyst can predict every factor. The goal is not perfection or improvement. The goal is to provide the best possible recommendation based on available evidence.

Effective decision-making does not require perfect information. It requires informed judgment.

A useful analysis acknowledges uncertainty instead of pretending it does not exist. In my opinion, admitting what we do not know can increase confidence in what we do know.

A practical view:

100% Certainty ✗

80% Confidence + Good Evidence ✓

The Human Side of Trust

Technology continues to transform analytics.

We have:

•	Dashboards
•	AI tools
•	Automation
•	Real-time reporting

Yet trust remains human.

Technology + Data + Human Judgment = Better Decisions

Technology can generate reports. Technology can display charts. Technology can summarize information. However, building trust still depends on people.

Two people can view the same dashboard:

Person A : Acts immediately

Person B : Requests more evidence

The dashboard is identical. Trust levels are different. This is why communication, credibility, and professional judgment remain essential skills for analysts.

Dashboards can display information, but people decide what to do with it.

Trust is a human decision, not a technical feature.

The human side of analytics is often overlooked, yet it may be one of the most important factors influencing whether data creates meaningful impact.

Conclusion

One of the most important lessons I have learned is that analytics is about more than numbers. Data provides evidence, but trust influences whether that evidence leads to action.

Successful analysts are not simply those who produce reports. They are the ones who consistently provide credible information and communicate it clearly.

Evidence 
↓
Credibility
↓
Confidence
↓
Action

When people trust the evidence, they gain confidence in the decisions built upon it.

Data informs decisions, but credibility influences whether those decisions are accepted.

The true measure of analytics is not how much information it produces, but how much confidence it creates.

Trust is the bridge between data and action.

Skills Strengthened

• Critical Thinking – Evaluating evidence objectively.

• Stakeholder Analysis – Interpreting data from multiple perspectives.

• Data Storytelling – Communicating insights effectively to stakeholders.

• Business Communication – Connecting analysis to business decisions.

• Problem Solving – Investigating unexpected findings and outcomes.

• Decision-Making Support – Supporting evidence-based recommendations.

• Professional Judgment – Making informed decisions under uncertainty.
title: Building Trust

content:
Can Anonymous Surveys Be Truly Anonymous?

Before studying Data Analytics at TRIOS College, I believed that successful analysis depended mainly on technical skills such as Excel, SQL, data visualization, and statistical methods. This week’s study of data ethics changed my perspective. I learned that even the most sophisticated analysis can produce misleading results if ethical concerns affect the quality of the data being collected.

One case that stood out involved a course evaluation survey. Students are required to log in using their username and password to access the survey, yet they are told that their responses will remain anonymous. As the data analyst responsible for providing recommendations to executive management, I must determine whether the survey data can be trusted and whether ethical concerns could affect the results.

This scenario highlights several important ethical concepts, including Privacy, Confidentiality, Trust, Transparency, Informed Consent, Bias, Accountability, and Data Integrity. More importantly, it demonstrates how ethics directly influences data quality and decision-making.

Ethical concerns can impact data quality long before an analyst begins working with the data.

Understanding the Problem

At first glance, the process appears straightforward. However, an ethical concern immediately emerges.

In this scenario:
•	Students complete a survey at the end of a course.
•	Students must log in using organizational credentials.
•	The survey asks for the course name but not the student's name.
•	The survey claims responses are anonymous.
•	Executive management uses the results to decide which courses require redesign or improvement.
•	The data analyst must provide actionable insights based on the survey results.

At first glance, the process appears straightforward. However, an ethical concern immediately emerges.

If students must log in before completing the survey, can they truly believe that their responses are anonymous?

Even if the organization has systems in place to separate login credentials from survey responses, participants may not understand how that process works.

Perception can influence behaviour just as strongly as reality when collecting data.

This concern forms the foundation for the four ethical questions explored below.

Course Survey Results
         ↓
Used by Executive Management
         ↓
Course Improvement Decisions

If survey responses are biased, the decisions based on those responses may also be flawed.

Question 1: Is the Survey Truly Anonymous?

The first ethical concern is whether the survey is anonymous or simply perceived as anonymous by the organization. From a technical perspective, it may be possible to separate authentication records from survey responses. However, data ethics requires us to consider the participant’s perspective as well.

Participants may ask: 
•	Can my responses be linked back to me?
•	Will negative feedback affect my standing?
•	Who can access my responses?
•	Is the anonymity claim accurate?

If students doubt anonymity, their behaviour may change.

For example:
•	They may avoid criticizing a course.
•	They may soften their feedback.
•	They may choose neutral responses instead of honest ones.
•	They may avoid participating altogether.
A survey can be technically anonymous, but if participants do not believe it is anonymous, their behaviour may change.

This demonstrates the importance of Privacy, Confidentiality, and Trust in ethical data collection.

Question 2: How Does Privacy and Trust Affect Data Quality?

Before this week’s learning, I viewed privacy mainly as a policy or compliance requirement. I now understand that privacy directly affects data quality.

1. Privacy

Privacy refers to an individual’s right to control how their information is collected, used, stored, and shared. In this scenario, students may be hesitant to provide honest responses because they are required to authenticate before accessing the survey.

2. Confidentiality

Confidentiality means ensuring that responses cannot be accessed, shared, or disclosed without authorization.

3. Trust

When participants believe their information is protected, they are more likely to provide genuine feedback.

Benefits include:
•	Increased participation
•	More honest responses
•	More representative data
•	Better decision-making

Privacy Protection
        ↓
Participant Trust
        ↓
Honest Responses
        ↓
Reliable Data

When trust increases, participants provide better data. When trust decreases, even a perfectly designed survey can produce unreliable results.

Trust
   ↓
Honest Responses
   ↓
Reliable Data
   ↓
Better Decisions

Trust is not a soft skill in analytics; it is a measurable factor that directly influences data quality.

Reduced Trust
        ↓
Response Bias
        ↓
Reduced Data Quality

Protecting privacy is not just about following policies; it is about creating an environment where people feel comfortable sharing honest feedback.

This was one of the most important lessons I learned from analyzing this scenario.

Question 3: What Ethical Risks Exist in This Scenario?

Several ethical concepts introduced this week apply directly to this case.

1. Lack of Transparency

Transparency requires organizations to clearly explain how participant information is collected, stored, and used. In this scenario, students may not understand:

•	Why login credentials are required
•	How anonymity is maintained
•	Whether identities can be linked to responses

A lack of transparency can reduce confidence in the survey process.

2. Weak Informed Consent

Informed Consent requires participants to understand what information is being collected and how it will be used. Participants should know:

•	Why the survey exists
•	Who will review the results
•	How anonymity is protected
•	How responses contribute to decision-making
3. Response Bias

Students who question anonymity may adjust their answers. Potential outcomes include:

•	Less criticism of course content
•	Underreporting concerns
•	Overuse of neutral responses
•	Incomplete feedback
4. Reduced Data Integrity

Data Integrity refers to the accuracy, consistency, and reliability of information. Biased responses may lead to inaccurate conclusions regarding course quality.

Unclear Anonymity
      ↓
Reduced Trust
      ↓
Altered Responses
      ↓
Response Bias
      ↓
Reduced Data Integrity

Not all data quality problems are technical; some begin with ethical concerns during data collection.

Reduced Data Integrity
            ↓
Misleading Conclusions
            ↓
Poor Business Decisions

The biggest risk is that management may believe the results accurately represent student opinions whereas, in reality, the ethical concerns may have influenced responses.

Question 4: What Should the Data Analyst Do?

• Accountability

One concept that resonated strongly with me this week was Accountability. As data analysts, our responsibilities extend beyond calculations, charts, and reports. We are also responsible for evaluating the ethical quality of the data we use. If I were assigned this project, I would take the following steps:

1. Verify Anonymity Procedures
•	Confirm how login credentials are separated from survey responses.
•	Validate that anonymity claims are accurate.
2. Improve Transparency

Recommend that participants receive clear explanations regarding:

•	Authentication requirements
•	Data storage practices
•	Access controls
•	Privacy protections
3. Identify Potential Bias

Evaluate whether anonymity concerns may affect participant behaviour.

4. Protect Confidential Information

Ensure survey data is only accessible to authorized individuals.

5. Report Findings Honestly

Present results objectively while acknowledging limitations.

6. Communicate Limitations

Explain factors that may affect reliability and interpretation.

Responsible Analytics = Transparency + Privacy Protection + Accountability + Data Integrity

As data analysts, our responsibility extends beyond analyzing numbers; we must also evaluate the ethical quality of the data behind those numbers.

Good analytics explains what the data says, while ethical analytics asks why the data may look that way.

• Limitations

If I were presenting findings to executive management, I would include an important limitation. Because participants must authenticate before accessing the survey, some students may question whether their responses are truly anonymous. This may result in:

•	Less critical feedback
•	Reduced participation
•	Underreporting of problems
•	Response bias

Therefore, survey findings should be interpreted carefully when making decisions about course redesign.

Perceived Lack of Anonymity
            ↓
Reduced Participation
            ↓
Incomplete Feedback
            ↓
Less Reliable Conclusions

Recognizing limitations does not weaken an analysis; it strengthens the credibility of the conclusions.

Every ethical decision made during data collection has the potential to improve or weaken the quality of the final analysis.

Including such limitations demonstrates both Transparency and Accountability.

• Personal Reflection

This assignment challenged my assumptions about data analysis. Prior to studying data ethics, I believed that accurate results depended primarily on technical expertise. I now realize that Privacy, Trust, Transparency, Confidentiality, Informed Consent, Bias, Data Integrity, and Accountability influence the quality of data long before analysis begins.

Ethical Decisions
        ↓
Better Data
        ↓
Better Insights
        ↓
Better Decisions

The most significant insight I gained was understanding the difference between actual anonymity and perceived anonymity.

As discussed in Martens (2022), Data Science Ethics: Concepts, Techniques, and Cautionary Tales, data professionals must consider not only what can be done with data, but also what should be done. This idea helped me understand that ethics is not separate from analytics; it is an essential part of responsible analytics and decision-making.

Even when a system is designed to protect participant identities, people may still modify their behaviour if they do not trust the process.

The most important insight I gained was understanding the difference between actual anonymity (objective approach where true identity is completely unknown) and perceived anonymity (subjective approach as it is a personal feeling or belief that the identity cannot be identified, even if it can be).

This case reminded me that every dataset represents real people, not just rows and columns in a spreadsheet.

Every dataset represents real people, and maintaining their trust is one of the most important responsibilities of a data analyst.

Every ethical decision made during data collection has the potential to improve or weaken the quality of the final analysis.

Conclusion

This scenario demonstrates how ethical considerations can influence participant behaviour, data quality, and organizational decision-making. Although the survey states that responses are anonymous, the requirement to log in may create uncertainty that affects trust and introduces response bias.

Through this week’s learning, I gained a deeper appreciation for the importance of Privacy, Confidentiality, Trust, Transparency, Informed Consent, Bias, Data Integrity, and Accountability in data analytics. These concepts are not separate from the analytical process; they are essential to producing reliable and meaningful insights.

As I continue my studies at TRIOS College, I aim to combine strong technical skills with strong ethical judgment. Data may drive decisions, but trust determines whether that data deserves to be trusted.

Data Quality = Accuracy + Completeness + Honesty

Strong analytical skills help us understand data, but strong ethical principles help us determine whether that data deserves to be trusted.

Understanding the problem

One of the most valuable lessons I have learned throughout my career is that successful analysis starts with understanding the problem. Before working with data, I focus on understanding business problem, objectives, stakeholder needs, and the decisions that need to be made.

Asking Questions

WHY ASKING BETTER QUESTIONS MATTERS MORE THAN HAVING THE RIGHT ANSWERS

What happened? Why did it happen? What should we do next?

Learning analytics reinforced what my experience had already taught me that asking the right questions often matters more than finding quick answers. Data can reveal what is happening, but thoughtful questions help uncover why it is happening.

The Insight

Insight = Data + Context + Curiosity

As I developed analytical skills, I discovered that data is only part of the story. Meaningful insights come from combining information with context, curiosity, and critical thinking.

Understanding the story

Whether reviewing stakeholder feedback, survey results, data spreadsheets or operational metrics, the real value comes from understanding the story behind the numbers.
